content.prompt: Find $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$ and $\tan\theta$ for each of the right-angled triangles shown below:

spec.description: Left vertical leg 3, bottom horizontal leg 4, right angle bottom left and theta bottom right. Decorative cyan fill omitted.
spec.mathematics: Opposite 3 and adjacent 4 relative to theta.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible.

answer.worked:
Let $h$ be the hypotenuse.
$$\begin{align*}h^2&=3^2+4^2\\h^2&=25\\h&=5\\\sin\theta&=\frac35\\\cos\theta&=\frac45\\\tan\theta&=\frac34\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Top horizontal leg 2, left vertical leg 3, right angle top left and theta top right. Decorative orange fill omitted.
spec.mathematics: Opposite 3 and adjacent 2 relative to theta.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible.

answer.worked:
Let $h$ be the hypotenuse.
$$\begin{align*}h^2&=3^2+2^2\\h^2&=13\\h&=\sqrt{13}\\\sin\theta&=\frac3{\sqrt{13}}=\frac{3\sqrt{13}}{13}\\\cos\theta&=\frac2{\sqrt{13}}=\frac{2\sqrt{13}}{13}\\\tan\theta&=\frac32\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Left vertical leg 0.6, bottom horizontal leg 0.8, right angle bottom left and theta bottom right. Decorative cyan fill omitted.
spec.mathematics: Opposite 0.6 and adjacent 0.8.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible.

answer.worked:
Let $h$ be the hypotenuse.
$$\begin{align*}h^2&=0.6^2+0.8^2\\h^2&=1\\h&=1\\\sin\theta&=\frac{0.6}{1}=0.6\\\cos\theta&=\frac{0.8}{1}=0.8\\\tan\theta&=\frac{0.6}{0.8}=0.75\end{align*}$$

spec.mathematics: Opposite 8 and adjacent 6.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible.

answer.worked:
Let $h$ be the hypotenuse.
$$\begin{align*}h^2&=8^2+6^2\\h^2&=100\\h&=10\\\sin\theta&=\frac8{10}=\frac45\\\cos\theta&=\frac6{10}=\frac35\\\tan\theta&=\frac86=\frac43\end{align*}$$

spec.mathematics: Adjacent leg is determined by Pythagoras.
spec.answerVisibility: The missing leg remains unlabelled.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the adjacent side.
$$\begin{align*}x^2+4^2&=6^2\\x^2&=20\\x&=2\sqrt5\\\sin\theta&=\frac46=\frac23\\\cos\theta&=\frac{2\sqrt5}{6}=\frac{\sqrt5}{3}\\\tan\theta&=\frac4{2\sqrt5}=\frac{2\sqrt5}{5}\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the opposite side.
$$\begin{align*}x^2+6^2&=7^2\\x^2&=13\\x&=\sqrt{13}\\\sin\theta&=\frac{\sqrt{13}}7\\\cos\theta&=\frac67\\\tan\theta&=\frac{\sqrt{13}}6\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the adjacent side.
$$\begin{align*}x^2+3^2&=6^2\\x^2&=27\\x&=3\sqrt3\\\sin\theta&=\frac36=\frac12\\\cos\theta&=\frac{3\sqrt3}{6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\\tan\theta&=\frac3{3\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
Let $h$ be the hypotenuse.
$$\begin{align*}h^2&=\left(\frac34\right)^2+\left(\frac23\right)^2\\h^2&=\frac9{16}+\frac49\\h^2&=\frac{145}{144}\\h&=\frac{\sqrt{145}}{12}\\\sin\theta&=\frac{3/4}{\sqrt{145}/12}=\frac{9\sqrt{145}}{145}\\\cos\theta&=\frac{2/3}{\sqrt{145}/12}=\frac{8\sqrt{145}}{145}\\\tan\theta&=\frac{3/4}{2/3}=\frac98\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Consider a right-angled triangle.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that the hypotenuse is always the longest side.

answer.short: $h=\sqrt{a^2+o^2}>a$ and $h>o$, since both legs are positive.
answer.worked:
Let the legs have lengths $a,o>0$ and the hypotenuse have length $h$. By Pythagoras,
$$\begin{align*}h&=\sqrt{a^2+o^2}\\h&>\sqrt{a^2}=a\\h&>\sqrt{o^2}=o\end{align*}$$
Thus the hypotenuse is longer than either leg.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Suppose that the triangle also contains an acute angle $\theta$. Prove that $0<\cos\theta<1$ and $0<\sin\theta<1$.

answer.worked:
Relative to the acute angle $\theta$, let $a$ and $o$ be the adjacent and opposite legs. Part (a) gives $0<a<h$ and $0<o<h$. Dividing by $h>0$ gives
$$0<\cos\theta=\frac ah<1,\qquad 0<\sin\theta=\frac oh<1.$$

teachingContext.mappingNote: Part (b) directly assesses the meaning and bounds of the ratio definitions.

content.prompt: The two right-triangles below have equal angles. In Theorem 1 we proved that $\frac oa=\frac OA$. Using this fact, additionally prove that $\frac oh=\frac OH$ and $\frac ah=\frac AH$.

spec.description: Smaller triangle at left, horizontal base a, vertical right leg o and hypotenuse h. Decorative cyan fill omitted.
spec.mathematics: Theta bottom left and right angle bottom right.
spec.answerVisibility: All supplied symbolic labels remain visible.

spec.description: Larger corresponding triangle at right, horizontal base A, vertical right leg O and hypotenuse H. Decorative orange fill omitted.
spec.mathematics: Theta bottom left and right angle bottom right; same shape as the smaller triangle.
spec.answerVisibility: All supplied symbolic labels remain visible.

answer.short:
$\frac oh=\frac OH$ and $\frac ah=\frac AH$.

Use $A=\frac{aO}{o}$ and Pythagoras to obtain $H=\frac{Oh}{o}$, then divide.
answer.worked:
The given equality gives $A=\frac{aO}{o}$, with all side lengths positive. By Pythagoras, $h^2=a^2+o^2$ and
$$\begin{align*}H&=\sqrt{A^2+O^2}\\H&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{aO}{o}\right)^2+O^2}\\H&=O\sqrt{\frac{a^2+o^2}{o^2}}\\H&=\frac{Oh}{o}.\end{align*}$$
Therefore,
$$\begin{align*}\frac OH&=\frac O{Oh/o}\\\frac OH&=\frac oh,\\\frac AH&=\frac{aO/o}{Oh/o}\\\frac AH&=\frac ah.\end{align*}$$

answer.short:

The flagpole is approximately $2.68\text{ m}$ tall.

content.prompt: A rope hangs from the top of a flag pole. The rope is 3 metres longer than the pole, and when it is pulled tight and held to the ground, the rope makes an angle of $50^\circ$ to the horizontal. How tall is the flag pole? Give your answer to two decimal places.

answer.worked:
Let $h$ metres be the height of the pole. The rope is the hypotenuse and has length $(h+3)$ metres.

$$\begin{align*}\sin50^\circ&=\frac{h}{h+3}\\(h+3)\sin50^\circ&=h\\h\sin50^\circ+3\sin50^\circ&=h\\h-h\sin50^\circ&=3\sin50^\circ\\h(1-\sin50^\circ)&=3\sin50^\circ\\h&=\frac{3\sin50^\circ}{1-\sin50^\circ}\\h&\approx9.82\end{align*}$$

The flag pole is $9.82\text{ m}$ tall.

content.prompt: A right-angled triangle has an angle $\theta$ and perimeter $P$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find a formula for the length of its hypotenuse in terms of $\theta$ and $P$.

answer.worked:
Let $L$ be the hypotenuse. The other sides have lengths $L\cos\theta$ and $L\sin\theta$.
$$\begin{align*}P&=L+L\cos\theta+L\sin\theta\\P&=L(1+\sin\theta+\cos\theta)\\L&=\frac{P}{1+\sin\theta+\cos\theta}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find a formula for the area of the triangle in terms of $\theta$ and $P$.

inlines.text: Use half the product of the perpendicular sides and substitute the hypotenuse from part (a).

answer.worked:
Using the hypotenuse $L$ from part (a),
$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac12(L\cos\theta)(L\sin\theta)\\A&=\frac12L^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\\A&=\frac12\left(\frac{P}{1+\sin\theta+\cos\theta}\right)^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\\A&=\frac{P^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{2(1+\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^2}.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Earth surface at left; paired tangent sight lines to the Moon at right, with a dashed centre line and dashed tangent radii. Ordinary marks are black and the diagram is unshaded.
spec.mathematics: The sight-line angle is theta. The centre line bisects it and has length d+r. Each tangent radius has length r and meets its sight line at a right angle. Coordinates derive both tangent points from a common centre and radius; construction proportions are illustrative.
spec.answerVisibility: All supplied labels and construction lines remain visible; no derived formula or numerical answer is drawn.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $r=\dfrac{d\sin(\theta/2)}{1-\sin(\theta/2)}$.

answer.worked:
The radius is perpendicular to the tangent sight line. The two right triangles are congruent, so the centre line bisects $\theta$.

$$\begin{align*}
\sin(\theta/2)&=\frac{r}{d+r}\\
(d+r)\sin(\theta/2)&=r\\
d\sin(\theta/2)+r\sin(\theta/2)&=r\\
r-r\sin(\theta/2)&=d\sin(\theta/2)\\
r\bigl(1-\sin(\theta/2)\bigr)&=d\sin(\theta/2)\\
r&=\frac{d\sin(\theta/2)}{1-\sin(\theta/2)}.
\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Given that $\theta=0.52^\circ$ and $d=384\,000$ kilometres, find $r$, to the nearest 10 kilometres.

answer.worked:

r&=\frac{384\,000\sin 0.26^\circ}{1-\sin 0.26^\circ}\\
r&\approx1750.474117\text{ km}\\
r&\approx1750\text{ km}\quad\text{(nearest 10 km)}.
\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Two externally tangent circles with collinear centres B and C and external point A. Their common upper tangent touches at D and E. Both tangent-radius right angles, radii 1 and 2, all five point labels and the angle at A are preserved. No shading.
spec.mathematics: BD=1, CE=2, BC=3; BD and CE are perpendicular to AE. Coordinates derive from sin(theta)=1/3 and produce exact tangencies.
spec.answerVisibility: Question diagram contains only source givens; no derived lengths or angle value are displayed.

inlines.text: Similar right triangles give AC = 2AB; the tangent circles give BC = 3, so AB = 3.

answer.worked:
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at its point of contact. Triangles $ABD$ and $ACE$ are therefore similar: both are right-angled and share the angle at $A$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{AC}{AB}&=\frac{CE}{BD}\\\frac{AC}{AB}&=2\\AC&=2AB\end{align*}$$
The circles touch externally, so $BC=1+2=3$ and $AC=AB+3$.
$$\begin{align*}2AB&=AB+3\\AB&=3\\\sin\theta&=\frac{BD}{AB}\\\sin\theta&=\frac{1}{3}\\\theta&=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\\\theta&\approx19.47^\circ\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Explain how the diagram below shows that $\tan^{-1}(1)+\tan^{-1}(2)+\tan^{-1}(3)=180^{\circ}$.

spec.description: Two columns and three rows of equal square cells, with a triangle joining the top-left corner, the bottom-edge midpoint and the right-edge point two cells above the bottom. The populated grid requires TikZ because the blank-grid template cannot express the triangle and angle sectors.
spec.mathematics: Vertices (0,3), (1,0), (2,2). Three adjacent sectors at (1,0) partition the upper straight angle.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied grid, triangle and unlabelled coloured sectors are visible; angle values and reasoning remain in answers.

answer.short:
The orange, blue and red angles are $\tan^{-1}(3)$, $\tan^{-1}(1)$ and $\tan^{-1}(2)$ respectively.

They partition a straight angle, so their sum is $180^{\circ}$. The blue angle is $45^{\circ}$ because the triangle is isosceles and right-angled.
answer.worked:
Each grid square has unit side length. The orange angle has opposite side $3$ and adjacent side $1$; the red angle has opposite side $2$ and adjacent side $1$.

$$\begin{align*}\tan(\text{orange angle})&=\frac{3}{1}=3\\\text{orange angle}&=\tan^{-1}(3)\\\tan(\text{red angle})&=\frac{2}{1}=2\\\text{red angle}&=\tan^{-1}(2)\end{align*}$$

From the triangle's rightmost vertex, the other two vertices are reached by moving two squares left and one up, or one square left and two down. These equal displacement patterns differ by a quarter-turn, so the two sides are equal and perpendicular. The triangle is therefore isosceles and right-angled.

$$\begin{align*}\text{blue angle}&=\frac{180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}}{2}\\\text{blue angle}&=45^{\circ}=\tan^{-1}(1)\end{align*}$$

The three coloured angles form a straight angle. Hence
$$\tan^{-1}(1)+\tan^{-1}(2)+\tan^{-1}(3)=180^{\circ}.$$

content.prompt: Explain how the diagram below shows that $\tan^{-1}(1)+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac12\right)+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac13\right)=90^\circ$.

spec.description: Two-column, three-row square grid with three joined vertices and three coloured sectors filling the bottom-left right angle. Free-form TikZ is required because the blank-grid template does not express the segments and angle sectors.
spec.mathematics: With bottom-left origin O, the other vertices are P=(1,3) and Q=(2,2). The three adjacent angles are atan(1), atan(1/2), and atan(1/3).
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied grid, segments and coloured sectors are visible; no angle values or added vertex labels are supplied.

answer.short: The red, blue and orange angles are respectively $\tan^{-1}(1)$, $\tan^{-1}(\frac12)$ and $\tan^{-1}(\frac13)$. They fill a right angle, so their sum is $90^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Let $O$ be the bottom-left corner, $P$ the upper vertex and $Q$ the right-hand vertex. Take each grid cell to have side length $1$.

For the red angle $\alpha$, the rise and run are both $2$:
$$\begin{align*}\tan\alpha&=\frac22=1\\\alpha&=\tan^{-1}(1).\end{align*}$$
For the orange angle $\gamma$, measured from the vertical, the opposite side is $1$ and the adjacent side is $3$:
$$\begin{align*}\tan\gamma&=\frac13\\\gamma&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac13\right).\end{align*}$$
The segments $OQ$ and $PQ$ are perpendicular: they follow diagonals of squares with opposite slopes. Also, $OQ=2\sqrt2$ and $PQ=\sqrt2$. Thus, for the blue angle $\beta$ in right-angled triangle $OPQ$,
$$\begin{align*}\tan\beta&=\frac{PQ}{OQ}\\\tan\beta&=\frac{\sqrt2}{2\sqrt2}=\frac12\\\beta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac12\right).\end{align*}$$
The three coloured angles fill the right angle at $O$. Therefore,
$$\tan^{-1}(1)+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac12\right)+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac13\right)=90^\circ.$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: The ball is struck at an angle of $\theta=40^\circ$ to the horizontal. Find the distance $x$ from the ball’s starting position to the location of the third bounce. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

answer.short:
$x\approx3.23$ table-length units.

Equal reflection angles give $x=8-\dfrac{4}{\tan40^\circ}$.
answer.worked:
Let $t$ be the horizontal distance from the starting corner to the first bounce. Equal reflection angles give the same acute angle to the horizontal on each segment.
$$\begin{align*}\tan40^\circ&=\frac{2}{t}\\t&=\frac{2}{\tan40^\circ}.\end{align*}$$
The horizontal distance from the first bounce to the right edge is $4-t$. Returning from the top edge to the bottom edge requires total horizontal travel $t$, so
$$\begin{align*}4-x&=t-(4-t)\\x&=8-2t\\x&=8-\frac{4}{\tan40^\circ}\\x&\approx3.23.\end{align*}$$
The distance is $3.23$ in the same units as the table dimensions.

children.label: b
children.prompt: The ball is struck so that $x=2$. Find the strike angle $\theta$, to 2 decimal places.

answer.short:
$\theta\approx33.69^\circ$.

Use equal reflection angles to obtain $\tan\theta=\dfrac{4}{8-x}$.
answer.worked:
Let $t$ be the horizontal distance to the first bounce. As in part (a), equal reflection angles give $x=8-2t$.
$$\begin{align*}2&=8-2t\\t&=3\\\tan\theta&=\frac{2}{3}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)\\\theta&\approx33.69^\circ.\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: What length of rope would ensure that the goat can access all of the grass in the field?

answer.worked:
The opposite corner is the farthest point from the tether.
$$\begin{align*}L^2&=30^2+40^2\\L^2&=2500\\L&=50\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: What percentage of the field’s area can the goat access if the length of the rope is 30 metres? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

answer.worked:
The accessible region is a quadrant of radius $30\text{ m}$.
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{field}}&=30\times40=1200\text{ m}^2\\A_{\text{accessible}}&=\frac14\pi(30)^2=225\pi\text{ m}^2\\\text{Percentage}&=\frac{225\pi}{1200}\times100\\\text{Percentage}&\approx58.90\%.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: What percentage of the field’s area can the goat access if the length of the rope is 35 metres? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

answer.short:
$75.09\%$

Subtract the circular segment beyond the 30 m boundary from the quadrant.
answer.worked:
Subtract the segment extending beyond the 30 m boundary. Let $\alpha$ be the angle between the perpendicular to that boundary and the radius to its intersection with the circle; let $s$ be the distance along the boundary from the perpendicular foot to that intersection.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{30}{35}\right)\\s&=\sqrt{35^2-30^2}=5\sqrt{13}\text{ m}\\A_{\text{segment}}&=\frac{\alpha}{360^{\circ}}\pi(35)^2-\frac12(30)(5\sqrt{13})\\A_{\text{accessible}}&=\frac14\pi(35)^2-A_{\text{segment}}\\A_{\text{accessible}}&\approx901.105636\text{ m}^2\\\text{Percentage}&=\frac{A_{\text{accessible}}}{1200}\times100\\\text{Percentage}&\approx75.09\%.\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: What percentage of the field’s area can the goat access if the length of the rope is 45 metres? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

answer.short:
$97.70\%$

Subtract the two circular segments beyond the 30 m and 40 m boundaries from the quadrant.
answer.worked:
The quadrant extends beyond both boundaries. The two outside segments do not overlap because the opposite corner is $50\text{ m}$ from the tether. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the angles between the perpendiculars to the respective boundaries and the radii to their circle intersections.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{30}{45}\right)\\\beta&=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{40}{45}\right)\\s_{30}&=\sqrt{45^2-30^2}=15\sqrt5\text{ m}\\s_{40}&=\sqrt{45^2-40^2}=5\sqrt{17}\text{ m}\\S_{30}&=\frac{\alpha}{360^{\circ}}\pi(45)^2-\frac12(30)(15\sqrt5)\\S_{40}&=\frac{\beta}{360^{\circ}}\pi(45)^2-\frac12(40)(5\sqrt{17})\\A_{\text{accessible}}&=\frac14\pi(45)^2-S_{30}-S_{40}\\A_{\text{accessible}}&\approx1172.444332\text{ m}^2\\\text{Percentage}&=\frac{A_{\text{accessible}}}{1200}\times100\\\text{Percentage}&\approx97.70\%.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A cylindrical glass of height 12 cm and diameter 8 cm is filled to the brim with water. The glass is carefully tilted so that its side makes an angle of $\theta$ to the horizontal. The glass is then carefully restored to an upright position.

spec.description: Superimposed upright and tilted open-glass side views share a lower contact point. The tilted sides are parallel, its water surface is horizontal through the lower rim, and its opposite side extends above that surface. Two restrained blue water fills preserve the instructional distinction.
spec.mathematics: The cylinder has height 12 cm and diameter 8 cm. Its axis makes angle theta with the horizontal. Diagram coordinates illustrate the geometry without supplying theta or any calculated height.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and the theta label are visible; no numerical answer is shown.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Given $\theta=50^\circ$, what is the new height of water in the glass? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

answer.short:
$8.64\text{ cm}$.

The upright height equals the mean retained depth measured parallel to the tilted glass's sides.
answer.worked:
Across the 8 cm diameter, the retained depth measured parallel to the glass's sides decreases by $8\cot\theta$. Symmetry of the circular cross-section gives a mean retained depth of $12-4\cot\theta$. The upright water height $h$ equals this mean depth because the volume is unchanged when the glass is restored.
$$\begin{align*}h&=12-\frac{4}{\tan\theta}\\h&=12-\frac{4}{\tan50^\circ}\\h&\approx8.64\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Given the new height of water in the glass is half the original height, find $\theta$. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

answer.worked:
Half the original height is $6\text{ cm}$. Using the mean retained depth,
$$\begin{align*}6&=12-\frac{4}{\tan\theta}\\\frac{4}{\tan\theta}&=6\\\tan\theta&=\frac{2}{3}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)\\\theta&\approx33.69^\circ.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A triangle with perimeter 10 has angles $30^{\circ}$, $60^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$. Find the area of the triangle.

answer.short:
$\dfrac{25(2\sqrt{3}-3)}{3}$ square units.

Use the side ratio $1:\sqrt{3}:2$, then calculate half the product of the perpendicular sides.
answer.worked:
The sides of a $30^{\circ}$–$60^{\circ}$–$90^{\circ}$ triangle are $k$, $k\sqrt{3}$ and $2k$.

$$\begin{align*}k+k\sqrt{3}+2k&=10\\k(3+\sqrt{3})&=10\\k&=\frac{10}{3+\sqrt{3}}\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac12 k(k\sqrt{3})\\A&=\frac{50\sqrt{3}}{(3+\sqrt{3})^2}\\A&=\frac{25\sqrt{3}}{3(2+\sqrt{3})}\\A&=\frac{25(2\sqrt{3}-3)}{3}\text{ square units}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Consider the figure shown below.

spec.description: Unfilled reconstruction retaining dashed AC and AD, solid BD and CD, equal-length ticks, labels and the right angle at C. Coordinates express a representative configuration without supplying a numerical angle.

spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that $\alpha=\dfrac{\theta}{2}$.

answer.worked:
Since $AB=BD$, triangle $ABD$ is isosceles, so $\angle ADB=\angle BAD=\alpha$. By the exterior angle theorem,
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=\angle BAD+\angle ADB\\\theta&=\alpha+\alpha\\\theta&=2\alpha.\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $\alpha=\dfrac{\theta}{2}$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, prove that $\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta}$.

answer.worked:
In right-angled triangle $BCD$, $BD=1$, so $CD=\sin\theta$ and $BC=\cos\theta$. Using part (a) and triangle $ACD$,
$$\begin{align*}\tan\frac{\theta}{2}&=\tan\alpha\\\tan\frac{\theta}{2}&=\frac{CD}{AC}\\\tan\frac{\theta}{2}&=\frac{CD}{AB+BC}\\\tan\frac{\theta}{2}&=\frac{\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Use the above formula to find the exact value of $\tan22.5^\circ$.

answer.short:
$\sqrt2-1$.

Substitute $\theta=45^\circ$ into the identity, then rationalise.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\tan22.5^\circ&=\frac{\sin45^\circ}{1+\cos45^\circ}\\\tan22.5^\circ&=\frac{1/\sqrt2}{1+1/\sqrt2}\\\tan22.5^\circ&=\frac{1}{\sqrt2+1}\\\tan22.5^\circ&=\frac{\sqrt2-1}{(\sqrt2+1)(\sqrt2-1)}\\\tan22.5^\circ&=\sqrt2-1.\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Use this to determine the area of a regular octagon of side length $1$.

answer.short:
$2+2\sqrt2$ square units.

Divide the octagon into eight congruent triangles and use $\tan22.5^\circ$ to find their perpendicular height.
answer.worked:
Join the centre to each vertex and bisect one of the eight congruent triangles. Its central half-angle is $22.5^\circ$, its half-base is $\tfrac12$, and its perpendicular height is $h$.
$$\begin{align*}\tan22.5^\circ&=\frac{1/2}{h}\\h&=\frac{1}{2\tan22.5^\circ}\\h&=\frac{1}{2(\sqrt2-1)}\\h&=\frac{\sqrt2+1}{2}.\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}A&=8\times\frac12\times1\times h\\A&=4\times\frac{\sqrt2+1}{2}\\A&=2+2\sqrt2\text{ square units}.\end{align*}$$

answer.short: $\angle ABF=\angle AFB=\angle DFE=\angle FDE=45^\circ$, $\angle FBD=60^\circ$, $\angle CBD=75^\circ$, $\angle CDB=15^\circ$. Each rectangle corner is $90^\circ$.
answer.worked:
$AB=AF$, so the right-angled triangle $ABF$ is isosceles. Thus $\angle ABF=\angle AFB=45^\circ$. Similarly, $FE=DE$ gives $\angle DFE=\angle FDE=45^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}\angle FBD&=180^\circ-90^\circ-30^\circ\\\angle FBD&=60^\circ\\\angle CBD&=180^\circ-45^\circ-60^\circ\\\angle CBD&=75^\circ\\\angle CDB&=180^\circ-90^\circ-75^\circ\\\angle CDB&=15^\circ\end{align*}$$

All four rectangle corners are $90^\circ$. The copied diagram is annotated below.

spec.description: Complete copied figure with every elementary missing angle annotated, including the rectangle corners.
spec.mathematics: Angles at B are 45°, 60°, 75°; at D they are 15°, 30°, 45°; at F they are 45°, 90°, 45°. Rectangle corners are right angles.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find lengths $AB$ and $DE$.

answer.worked:
Use the two $45^\circ$ right-angled triangles.

$$\begin{align*}AB&=BF\sin45^\circ\\AB&=1\times\frac1{\sqrt2}\\AB&=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\\DE&=FD\sin45^\circ\\DE&=\sqrt3\times\frac1{\sqrt2}\\DE&=\frac{\sqrt6}{2}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence, find lengths $BC$ and $CD$.

answer.worked:
Opposite sides of the rectangle are equal, and the marked isosceles triangles give $AF=AB$ and $FE=DE$.

$$\begin{align*}BC&=AC-AB\\BC&=\frac{\sqrt6}{2}-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\\BC&=\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{2}\\CD&=AF+FE\\CD&=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+\frac{\sqrt6}{2}\\CD&=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{2}\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Hence, find the exact values of $\sin15^\circ$, $\cos15^\circ$, $\sin75^\circ$ and $\cos75^\circ$.

answer.worked:
In right-angled triangle $BCD$, $BD=2$, $\angle CDB=15^\circ$ and $\angle CBD=75^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}\sin15^\circ&=\frac{BC}{BD}\\\sin15^\circ&=\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}\\\cos15^\circ&=\frac{CD}{BD}\\\cos15^\circ&=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\\\sin75^\circ&=\frac{CD}{BD}\\\sin75^\circ&=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\\\cos75^\circ&=\frac{BC}{BD}\\\cos75^\circ&=\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: A piece of string of length 1 metre is tightly wrapped around a right-angled triangle with angles $15^\circ$, $75^\circ$ and $90^\circ$. Find the exact length of the triangle’s hypotenuse.

answer.short:
$(\sqrt6-2)\text{ m}$.

Express both shorter sides as multiples of the hypotenuse and use the perimeter of 1 metre.
answer.worked:
Let the hypotenuse be $x$ metres. The shorter sides are $x\sin15^\circ$ and $x\cos15^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}1&=x+x\sin15^\circ+x\cos15^\circ\\1&=x\left(1+\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}+\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\right)\\1&=x\left(1+\frac{\sqrt6}{2}\right)\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}x&=\frac{2}{2+\sqrt6}\\x&=\frac{2(\sqrt6-2)}{(\sqrt6+2)(\sqrt6-2)}\\x&=\sqrt6-2\end{align*}$$

The hypotenuse is $(\sqrt6-2)\text{ m}$.

children.label: f
children.prompt: Hence, find the exact area of a regular dodecagon of side length 1.

answer.short:
$6+3\sqrt3$ square units.

Divide the dodecagon into 24 right triangles with base $\tfrac12$ and central angle $15^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Join the centre to each vertex, then bisect each of the 12 congruent triangles. This gives 24 right triangles, each with central angle $15^\circ$, base $\tfrac12$ and height $h$.

$$\begin{align*}\tan15^\circ&=\frac{1/2}{h}\\h&=\frac1{2\tan15^\circ}\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}A&=24\times\frac12\times\frac12\times\frac1{2\tan15^\circ}\\A&=\frac3{\tan15^\circ}\\A&=\frac{3(\sqrt6+\sqrt2)}{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}\\A&=\frac{3(\sqrt6+\sqrt2)^2}{6-2}\\A&=\frac{3(8+4\sqrt3)}4\\A&=6+3\sqrt3\end{align*}$$

The area is $6+3\sqrt3$ square units.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Copy the diagram, and then determine all of the missing angles.

answer.short:
$\angle EAD=\angle DAC=\angle CAB=36^\circ$; $\angle ABD=72^\circ$, $\angle DBC=36^\circ$; $\angle BCA=36^\circ$, $\angle ACD=72^\circ$; $\angle EDA=\angle ADB=\angle BDC=36^\circ$; $\angle AED=108^\circ$.

At $P$: $\angle APB=\angle CPD=72^\circ$ and $\angle BPC=\angle DPA=108^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Each interior angle of the regular pentagon is $108^\circ$. Its diagonals are equal.

Since $AB=BC$, $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles:
$$\begin{align*}\angle BAC&=\frac{180^\circ-108^\circ}{2}\\\angle BAC&=36^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Similarly, $\angle BCA=\angle EAD=\angle EDA=36^\circ$. Subtracting these from the interior angles gives:
$$\begin{align*}\angle DAC&=108^\circ-36^\circ-36^\circ=36^\circ\\\angle ACD&=108^\circ-36^\circ=72^\circ.\end{align*}$$

In $\triangle BCD$, $BC=CD$, so $\angle DBC=\angle BDC=36^\circ$. Hence $\angle ABD=72^\circ$ and $\angle ADB=36^\circ$.

In $\triangle ABP$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle APB&=180^\circ-36^\circ-72^\circ\\\angle APB&=72^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Vertically opposite angles give $\angle CPD=72^\circ$. Adjacent angles on a straight line give $\angle BPC=\angle DPA=108^\circ$. The completed diagram shows every elementary angle.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that triangles $\triangle ADC$ and $\triangle DCP$ are similar.

answer.short: $\triangle ADC\sim\triangle DCP$ by AAA: corresponding angles are $36^\circ$, $72^\circ$ and $72^\circ$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle DAC&=\angle CDP=36^\circ\\\angle ADC&=\angle DCP=72^\circ\\\angle ACD&=\angle DPC=72^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle ADC\sim\triangle DCP$ by AAA, with $A\leftrightarrow D$, $D\leftrightarrow C$ and $C\leftrightarrow P$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence, find the length of the diagonal $AD$.

answer.worked:
Let $x=AD=AC$. In $\triangle ABP$, equal angles at $B$ and $P$ give $AP=AB=1$. Thus $CP=x-1$.

Using the corresponding sides of $\triangle ADC$ and $\triangle DCP$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{1}&=\frac{1}{x-1}\\x(x-1)&=1\\x^2-x-1&=0\\x&=\frac{1\pm\sqrt5}{2}\\AD&=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}.\end{align*}$$
The negative root is rejected because a length is positive.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find the exact values of $\sin18^\circ$, $\cos18^\circ$, $\sin72^\circ$ and $\cos72^\circ$.

answer.worked:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $DC$. Since $AD=AC$, $AM\perp DC$ and $\angle DAM=18^\circ$. Here $DM=\tfrac12$ and $AD=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$.
$$\begin{align*}\sin18^\circ&=\frac{DM}{AD}\\\sin18^\circ&=\frac{1}{1+\sqrt5}\\\sin18^\circ&=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4}.\end{align*}$$
Pythagoras in the same right triangle gives:
$$\begin{align*}\cos^2 18^\circ&=1-\left(\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4}\right)^2\\\cos^2 18^\circ&=\frac{5+\sqrt5}{8}\\\cos18^\circ&=\sqrt{\frac{5+\sqrt5}{8}}.\end{align*}$$
The other acute angle is $72^\circ$, so:
$$\begin{align*}\sin72^\circ&=\cos18^\circ=\sqrt{\frac{5+\sqrt5}{8}}\\\cos72^\circ&=\sin18^\circ=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: Find the exact values of $\sin36^\circ$, $\cos36^\circ$, $\sin54^\circ$ and $\cos54^\circ$.

answer.worked:
Let $N$ be the midpoint of $AC$. Since $AB=BC=1$, $BN\perp AC$, $\angle BAN=36^\circ$ and $AN=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{4}$.
$$\begin{align*}\cos36^\circ&=\frac{AN}{AB}\\\cos36^\circ&=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{4}.\end{align*}$$
Pythagoras in $\triangle ABN$ gives:
$$\begin{align*}\sin^2 36^\circ&=1-\left(\frac{1+\sqrt5}{4}\right)^2\\\sin^2 36^\circ&=\frac{5-\sqrt5}{8}\\\sin36^\circ&=\sqrt{\frac{5-\sqrt5}{8}}.\end{align*}$$
The other acute angle is $54^\circ$, so:
$$\begin{align*}\sin54^\circ&=\cos36^\circ=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{4}\\\cos54^\circ&=\sin36^\circ=\sqrt{\frac{5-\sqrt5}{8}}.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle; the two chords from A are highlighted.
spec.mathematics: Circle radius 1; vertices A, B, C in clockwise order, separated by central angles of 120 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied geometry and vertex labels are visible.

answer.short:
$AB=AC=\sqrt3$, so $AB\times AC=3$.

Bisect a central triangle and use $\sin60^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Join the centre $O$ to $A$ and $B$. Then $\angle AOB=120^\circ$. The perpendicular from $O$ to $AB$ bisects both the chord and this angle. Since the radius is 1,
$$\begin{align*}AB&=2\sin60^\circ\\AB&=2\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\\AB&=\sqrt3.\end{align*}$$
The equilateral triangle has $AC=AB$. Thus
$$AB\times AC=\sqrt3\times\sqrt3=3.$$

children.label: b

The vertices $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ of a square lie on a circle of radius 1. Show that
$$AB\times AC\times AD=4.$$

spec.description: Inscribed square with highlighted AB and AD, and separately highlighted diameter AC.
spec.mathematics: Circle radius 1; consecutive vertices separated by central angles of 90 degrees; AC is a diameter.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied geometry and vertex labels are visible.

answer.worked:
$AC$ is a diameter, so $AC=2$. Triangle $ABC$ is a $45^\circ$–$45^\circ$–$90^\circ$ triangle. Hence
$$\begin{align*}AB&=2\sin45^\circ\\AB&=\sqrt2.\end{align*}$$
The square has $AD=AB$. Therefore
$$AB\times AC\times AD=\sqrt2\times2\times\sqrt2=4.$$

answer.short:
$AB\times AC\times AD\times AE=5$.

Use the exact values from exercise 6 to obtain $AB^2=(5-\sqrt5)/2$ and $AC^2=(5+\sqrt5)/2$.
answer.worked:
The central angles for $AB$ and $AC$ are $72^\circ$ and $144^\circ$. Bisecting the corresponding isosceles triangles gives $AB=2\sin36^\circ$ and $AC=2\sin72^\circ$. Using exercise 6,
$$AB=AE=\sqrt{\frac{5-\sqrt5}{2}},\qquad AC=AD=\sqrt{\frac{5+\sqrt5}{2}}.$$

answer.worked:
Each central angle between consecutive vertices is $60^\circ$, so the triangles formed by two adjacent radii are equilateral. Hence $AB=AF=1$. Also, $AD$ is a diameter, so $AD=2$. Bisecting the $120^\circ$ central triangle gives

content.prompt: For $\triangle ABC$ we are given that $a=6$, $\angle A=30^\circ$ and $\angle B=45^\circ$. Find the area of the triangle.

answer.short:
$(9\sqrt{3}+9)$ square units.

Find $AC$ using the sine rule, then drop a perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$ and use half the base times the height.
answer.worked:
Using the sine rule,
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{b}{\sin45^\circ}&=\frac{6}{\sin30^\circ}\\
b&=\frac{6\sin45^\circ}{\sin30^\circ}\\
b&=6\sqrt2.
\end{align*}$$
Let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$. Since $A=30^\circ$ and $B=45^\circ$, $D$ lies between $A$ and $B$.
$$\begin{align*}
CD&=AC\sin30^\circ=3\sqrt2\\
AD&=AC\cos30^\circ=3\sqrt6\\
BD&=CD=3\sqrt2\\
AB&=AD+BD=3\sqrt6+3\sqrt2.
\end{align*}$$
Therefore,
$$\begin{align*}
\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac12 AB\cdot CD\\
&=\frac12(3\sqrt6+3\sqrt2)(3\sqrt2)\\
&=9\sqrt3+9.
\end{align*}$$
The area is $(9\sqrt3+9)$ square units.

content.prompt:
For $\triangle ABC$ shown below,
$$\begin{aligned}AD:DB&=1:1\\BE:EC&=3:7\\CF:FA&=1:2.\end{aligned}$$
Given that $\operatorname{area}(\triangle DEF)=5$, find $\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)$.

spec.description: Triangle ABC with horizontal AC and interior triangle DEF. Coordinates reconstruct the stated division ratios; they are not additional givens. The source cyan fill is intentionally omitted under the house outline convention.
spec.mathematics: D is the midpoint of AB; BE/BC=3/10; CF/CA=1/3. All six vertex labels and the three inner edges are retained.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied geometry and labels are visible; no calculated area or solution annotation is included.

answer.short:
$\dfrac{300}{17}$ square units.

Subtract the three corner-triangle areas; $\triangle DEF$ occupies $\dfrac{17}{60}$ of $\triangle ABC$.
answer.worked:
Let $S=\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)$. Triangles sharing an included angle have area ratios equal to the products of the corresponding adjacent-side ratios.
$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{area}(\triangle ADF)&=\frac{AD}{AB}\frac{AF}{AC}S\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle ADF)&=\frac12\cdot\frac23S=\frac13S\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle BDE)&=\frac{BD}{BA}\frac{BE}{BC}S\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle BDE)&=\frac12\cdot\frac3{10}S=\frac3{20}S\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle CEF)&=\frac{CE}{CB}\frac{CF}{CA}S\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle CEF)&=\frac7{10}\cdot\frac13S=\frac7{30}S\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle DEF)&=S-\frac13S-\frac3{20}S-\frac7{30}S\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle DEF)&=\frac{17}{60}S.\end{align*}$$
Since the inner area is 5,
$$\begin{align*}S&=5\cdot\frac{60}{17}\\S&=\frac{300}{17}\text{ square units}.\end{align*}$$

$\angle C_1=39^\circ$ and $\angle C_2=141^\circ$.

Use the sine rule and the supplementary angle.
answer.worked:
By the sine rule,
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{\sin C}{6}&=\frac{\sin25^\circ}{4}\\
\sin C&=\frac{6\sin25^\circ}{4}\\
C_1&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{6\sin25^\circ}{4}\right)\\
C_1&\approx39.3405^\circ\\
C_2&=180^\circ-\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{6\sin25^\circ}{4}\right)\\
C_2&\approx140.6595^\circ.
\end{align*}$$
Both angles give $A+C<180^\circ$, so both triangles are possible. To the nearest degree, $\angle C_1=39^\circ$ and $\angle C_2=141^\circ$.

content.prompt: Show that there are two possible triangles $\triangle ABC$ for which $a=6$, $c=9$ and $\angle A=30^\circ$. Find the two possible measures of $\angle C$, correct to the nearest degree.

answer.short:
$\angle C=49^\circ$ or $131^\circ$.

The sine rule gives supplementary angles, and both leave a positive third angle.
answer.worked:
Here $c\sin A=9\sin30^\circ=4.5$, so $c\sin A<a<c$. Hence two triangles are possible.

Using the sine rule,
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{\sin C}{9}&=\frac{\sin30^\circ}{6}\\
\sin C&=\frac{9\sin30^\circ}{6}\\
\sin C&=\frac34\\
C_1&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac34\right)\\
C_1&\approx48.59^\circ\\
C_2&=180^\circ-\sin^{-1}\left(\frac34\right)\\
C_2&\approx131.41^\circ.
\end{align*}$$
Both values are less than $150^\circ$, so both leave a positive angle $B=180^\circ-30^\circ-C$.

Therefore $\angle C=49^\circ$ or $131^\circ$, to the nearest degree.

content.prompt: To find the height of a mountaintop, a surveyor takes measurements from two accessible points $A$ and $B$ as shown below. Find the height $h$ of the mountain, correct to the nearest metre.

spec.description: Horizontal baseline A–B–C, vertical CD, sight lines AD and BD, and a right-angle mark at C. Decorative mountain silhouette and shading omitted.
spec.mathematics: AB = 321 m; angle DAC = 31 degrees; angle DBC = 47 degrees; CD = h. Coordinates derive the two sight-line angles exactly.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and the unknown h are visible.

answer.short:
$439\text{ m}$.

Use the sine rule in $\triangle ABD$, then $h=BD\sin47^\circ$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
\angle ABD &= 180^\circ-47^\circ=133^\circ\\
\angle ADB &= 180^\circ-31^\circ-133^\circ=16^\circ
\end{align*}$$
By the sine rule in $\triangle ABD$,
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{BD}{\sin31^\circ} &= \frac{321}{\sin16^\circ}\\
BD &= \frac{321\sin31^\circ}{\sin16^\circ}.
\end{align*}$$
In right-angled $\triangle BCD$,
$$\begin{align*}
h &= BD\sin47^\circ\\
h &= \frac{321\sin31^\circ\sin47^\circ}{\sin16^\circ}\\
h &\approx 438.6658\text{ m}.
\end{align*}$$
The height of the mountain is $439\text{ m}$, to the nearest metre.

answer.worked:
Let $T$ be the balloon position and let $BT=x$ metres.
$$\begin{align*}
\angle ABT&=180^\circ-70^\circ\\
\angle ABT&=110^\circ\\
\angle ATB&=180^\circ-35^\circ-110^\circ\\

$$\begin{align*}
\frac{x}{\sin35^\circ}&=\frac{150}{\sin35^\circ}\\
x&=150.
\end{align*}$$
Using the right triangle beneath the balloon,

h&\approx140.953893.

content.prompt: For $\triangle ABC$ we are given that $c=6$ and $\angle A=25^\circ$. Find the value(s) of $a$ for which there is only one such triangle.

answer.short:
$a=6\sin25^\circ$ or $a\ge6$.

The height boundary gives one right-angled triangle; equal or longer opposite sides give one triangle.
answer.worked:
The limiting height is
$$\begin{align*}h&=c\sin A\\h&=6\sin25^\circ.\end{align*}$$
If $a<h$, no triangle exists. If $a=h$, exactly one right-angled triangle exists. If $h<a<6$, two triangles exist.

When $a=6$, the sine rule gives $C=25^\circ$ or $155^\circ$. The latter gives $B=0^\circ$, so only $C=25^\circ$, $B=130^\circ$ is valid.

When $a>6$,
$$\sin C=\frac{6\sin25^\circ}{a}<\sin25^\circ.$$
The acute solution has $C<25^\circ$; its supplementary solution has $C>155^\circ$ and cannot form a triangle with $A=25^\circ$. Thus exactly one triangle exists.

Therefore $a=6\sin25^\circ$ or $a\ge6$.

content.prompt: Find all possible areas of a triangle with two sides of length $10$ and $11$, and one angle of $60^\circ$, correct to two decimal places.

inlines.text: Consider the included angle and the angle opposite each given side; use both valid sine-rule solutions.

answer.worked:
Let $K$ be the area. The $60^\circ$ angle can lie between the given sides or opposite either given side.

If it is the included angle:
$$\begin{align*}K&=\frac12(10)(11)\sin60^\circ\\K&\approx47.63\text{ units}^2.\end{align*}$$

If it is opposite the side of length $10$, let $B$ be opposite the side of length $11$:
$$\begin{align*}\sin B&=\frac{11\sin60^\circ}{10}\\B&=\alpha\text{ or }180^\circ-\alpha,\qquad \alpha=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{11\sin60^\circ}{10}\right).\end{align*}$$
Both choices give a positive third angle. The included angle is $120^\circ-\alpha$ or $\alpha-60^\circ$:
$$\begin{align*}K&=55\sin(120^\circ-\alpha)\approx40.68\text{ units}^2\\K&=55\sin(\alpha-60^\circ)\approx11.71\text{ units}^2.\end{align*}$$

If it is opposite the side of length $11$, let $B$ be opposite the side of length $10$:
$$\begin{align*}\sin B&=\frac{10\sin60^\circ}{11}\\B&=\beta,\qquad\beta=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{10\sin60^\circ}{11}\right).\end{align*}$$
Here $\beta<60^\circ$, so the supplementary choice would make the angle sum exceed $180^\circ$. Thus:
$$\begin{align*}K&=55\sin(120^\circ-\beta)\\K&\approx51.02\text{ units}^2.\end{align*}$$

The possible areas are $11.71$, $40.68$, $47.63$ and $51.02\text{ units}^2$. All calculations use unrounded angles.

content.prompt:
In this exercise we’ll give an alternative proof of the sine rule. Use the formula for the area of a triangle introduced in the previous section to prove that
$$\frac{2}{abc}\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)=\frac{\sin A}{a}=\frac{\sin B}{b}=\frac{\sin C}{c}.$$

answer.short:
$$\frac{2}{abc}\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)=\frac{\sin A}{a}=\frac{\sin B}{b}=\frac{\sin C}{c}.$$

Apply the area rule at each vertex and divide each expression by $abc/2$.
answer.worked:
Applying the area rule at each vertex gives
$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac12bc\sin A\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac12ca\sin B\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac12ab\sin C.
\end{align*}$$
Multiplying each expression by $\dfrac{2}{abc}$ gives
$$\begin{align*}\frac{2}{abc}\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac{\sin A}{a}\\\frac{2}{abc}\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac{\sin B}{b}\\\frac{2}{abc}\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac{\sin C}{c}.
\end{align*}$$
Thus all four expressions are equal, as required.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Suppose $\angle A,\angle B\leq90^\circ$. With the aid of a diagram explain why
$$\angle A\leq\angle B\iff\sin(A)\leq\sin(B).$$

answer.short: For right triangles with hypotenuse $1$, the opposite side has length $\sin\theta$. As the acute angle increases, this side increases, so the stated equivalence holds, including equality.
answer.worked:
Draw two right triangles with a common initial ray and hypotenuses of length $1$, as shown. The vertical sides have lengths $\sin A$ and $\sin B$. On the quarter-circle of radius $1$, the height increases strictly as the angle increases from $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$. Thus the smaller angle has the smaller opposite side, and conversely. Equal angles give equal opposite sides. Hence
$$\angle A\leq\angle B\iff\sin A\leq\sin B.$$

spec.sourceRegion: Question 17(a); answer figure on teacher PDF page 13
spec.description: Two overlapping right triangles with a common initial ray and unit hypotenuses, illustrating a smaller and a larger acute angle. Illustrative coordinates are not numerical givens.
spec.mathematics: Unit hypotenuses make the perpendicular opposite sides equal to sin A and sin B; A is illustrated smaller than B.
spec.answerVisibility: Solution only; the student must supply a diagram.

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Hence, prove that
$$\angle A\leq\angle B\iff\sin(A)\leq\sin(B)$$
whenever $\angle A$ and $\angle B$ are (possibly obtuse) angles in a triangle.

answer.short: Use part (a), $A+B<180^\circ$ and $\sin(180^\circ-\theta)=\sin\theta$ to prove both directions, treating an obtuse angle through its acute supplement.
answer.worked:
Angles in a triangle satisfy $A+B<180^\circ$.

First suppose $A\leq B$. If $B\leq90^\circ$, part (a) gives $\sin A\leq\sin B$. If $B>90^\circ$, then $A<180^\circ-B<90^\circ$, so part (a) gives
$$\sin A<\sin(180^\circ-B)=\sin B.$$

Conversely, suppose $\sin A\leq\sin B$. If $A>90^\circ$, then $B<180^\circ-A<90^\circ$. Part (a) would give $\sin B<\sin(180^\circ-A)=\sin A$, a contradiction. Thus $A\leq90^\circ$. If $B\leq90^\circ$, part (a) gives $A\leq B$. If $B>90^\circ$, then $A\leq90^\circ<B$.

Therefore
$$A\leq B\iff\sin A\leq\sin B.$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Given $\triangle ABC$, prove that $a\leq b\leq c$ if and only if $\angle A\leq\angle B\leq\angle C$.

answer.short: The sine rule gives $a/b=\sin A/\sin B$. Thus $a\leq b$ is equivalent to $\sin A\leq\sin B$, and hence to $A\leq B$ by part (b). Apply the same argument to $b$ and $c$.
answer.worked:
By the sine rule,
$$\frac{a}{b}=\frac{\sin A}{\sin B}.$$
Since $b>0$ and $\sin B>0$,
$$\begin{aligned}
a\leq b&\iff\frac{a}{b}\leq1\\
a\leq b&\iff\frac{\sin A}{\sin B}\leq1\\
a\leq b&\iff\sin A\leq\sin B\\
a\leq b&\iff A\leq B.
\end{aligned}$$
The last equivalence follows from part (b). Similarly, $b\leq c$ if and only if $B\leq C$. Combining the two equivalences gives
$$a\leq b\leq c\iff A\leq B\leq C.$$

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Assuming the sine rule, prove that
$$\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C}=2R.$$

answer.short:
$\dfrac{a}{\sin A}=\dfrac{b}{\sin B}=\dfrac{c}{\sin C}=2R$.

Bisect the central angle subtended by $BC$, then apply the sine rule.
answer.worked:
Join $O$ to $B$ and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Since $OB=OC=R$, $OM$ bisects $\angle BOC$ and is perpendicular to $BC$. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so $\angle BOC=2A$ and $\angle BOM=A$.
$$\begin{align*}\sin A&=\frac{BM}{OB}\\\sin A&=\frac{a}{2R}\\\frac{a}{\sin A}&=2R.\end{align*}$$
The sine rule now gives
$$\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C}=2R.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Hence, show that
$$\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)=\frac{abc}{4R}.$$

answer.short:
$\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)=\dfrac{abc}{4R}$.

Substitute $\sin C=\dfrac{c}{2R}$ into the triangle area rule.
answer.worked:
From part (a), $\sin C=\dfrac{c}{2R}$.
$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac12 ab\sin C\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac12 ab\left(\frac{c}{2R}\right)\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac{abc}{4R}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt:
If $r$ is the inradius of $\triangle ABC$, then show that
$$\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)=\frac{(a+b+c)r}{2}.$$

answer.short:
$\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)=\dfrac{(a+b+c)r}{2}$.

Join the incentre to the vertices and add the three triangle areas.
answer.worked:
Join the incentre to $A$, $B$ and $C$. The three resulting triangles have bases $a$, $b$ and $c$, each with perpendicular height $r$.
$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac12 ar+\frac12 br+\frac12 cr\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac{(a+b+c)r}{2}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt:
Hence, prove that
$$rR=\frac{abc}{2(a+b+c)}.$$

answer.short:
$rR=\dfrac{abc}{2(a+b+c)}$.

Equate the area formulas from parts (b) and (c).
answer.worked:
Parts (b) and (c) give
$$\begin{align*}\frac{(a+b+c)r}{2}&=\frac{abc}{4R}\\(a+b+c)rR&=\frac{abc}{2}\\rR&=\frac{abc}{2(a+b+c)}.\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$0$.

By the sine rule, write $a=k\sin A$, $b=k\sin B$ and $c=k\sin C$; the six product terms cancel in pairs.
answer.worked:
By the sine rule, write $a=k\sin A$, $b=k\sin B$ and $c=k\sin C$ for a constant $k$. Let
$$E=a(\sin B-\sin C)+b(\sin C-\sin A)+c(\sin A-\sin B).$$
Substituting and expanding,
$$\begin{aligned}E={}&k\bigl[\sin A(\sin B-\sin C)\\&{}+\sin B(\sin C-\sin A)\\&{}+\sin C(\sin A-\sin B)\bigr]\\={}&k\bigl[\sin A\sin B-\sin A\sin C\\&{}+\sin B\sin C-\sin B\sin A\\&{}+\sin C\sin A-\sin C\sin B\bigr]\\={}&0.\end{aligned}$$
The six product terms cancel in pairs.

Use $\sin A=ka$, $\sin B=kb$ and $\sin C=kc$ from the sine rule; the expanded terms cancel.
answer.worked:
By the sine rule,
$$\frac{\sin A}{a}=\frac{\sin B}{b}=\frac{\sin C}{c}=k.$$
Thus $\sin A=ka$, $\sin B=kb$ and $\sin C=kc$. Let $E=(b-c)\sin A+(c-a)\sin B+(a-b)\sin C$. Then

content.prompt: Find a formula for the area of the triangle in terms of its three angles $A$, $B$ and $C$, and its perimeter $P$. Hint: start by writing $P=a+b+c$, and then use the sine rule.

answer.short:
$$\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)=\frac{P^2\sin A\sin B\sin C}{2(\sin A+\sin B+\sin C)^2}.$$

Use the sine rule to express the sides in terms of one side, then substitute the perimeter into the area rule.
answer.worked:
By the sine rule,
$$b=\frac{a\sin B}{\sin A},\qquad c=\frac{a\sin C}{\sin A}.$$
Thus
$$\begin{align*}P&=a+b+c\\P&=a\left(1+\frac{\sin B}{\sin A}+\frac{\sin C}{\sin A}\right)\\P&=\frac{a(\sin A+\sin B+\sin C)}{\sin A}.\end{align*}$$
Hence
$$a=\frac{P\sin A}{\sin A+\sin B+\sin C}.$$
Using the area rule,
$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac12 ab\sin C\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac{a^2\sin B\sin C}{2\sin A}\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac{P^2\sin A\sin B\sin C}{2(\sin A+\sin B+\sin C)^2}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A point is located in a square such that it is 3 m from one corner, 4 m from another corner, and 5 m from a third corner (in clockwise order). Find the area of the square.

answer.short:
$(17+4\sqrt{14})\text{ m}^2$.

Apply the cosine rule twice and use the complementary angles at the middle corner.
answer.worked:
Let the square have consecutive vertices $A,B,C,D$, side length $x$ metres and interior point $P$, where $PA=3$, $PB=4$ and $PC=5$. Let $\alpha=\angle ABP$ and $\beta=\angle PBC$. Since $\alpha+\beta=90^\circ$, $\cos^2\alpha+\cos^2\beta=1$.

The cosine rule gives
$$\begin{align*}3^2&=x^2+4^2-2(x)(4)\cos\alpha\\5^2&=x^2+4^2-2(x)(4)\cos\beta\\\cos\alpha&=\frac{x^2+7}{8x}\\\cos\beta&=\frac{x^2-9}{8x}.\end{align*}$$
Substituting into the identity,
$$\begin{align*}\left(\frac{x^2+7}{8x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{x^2-9}{8x}\right)^2&=1\\(x^2+7)^2+(x^2-9)^2&=64x^2\\2x^4-68x^2+130&=0\\x^4-34x^2+65&=0\\x^2&=\frac{34\pm\sqrt{34^2-4(65)}}{2}\\x^2&=17\pm4\sqrt{14}.\end{align*}$$
The distance from a point in the square to a corner cannot exceed the diagonal, so $5\le x\sqrt2$, giving $x^2\ge25/2$. This excludes $17-4\sqrt{14}$.

Therefore, the area is $(17+4\sqrt{14})\text{ m}^2$.

content.prompt: The law of cosines can be regarded as a generalisation of the Pythagorean Theorem to non-right-angled triangles, since it reduces to this theorem in the case where $\angle C=90^\circ$. Explain whether $a^2+b^2$ is larger or smaller than $c^2$ when $\angle C$ is:

answer.worked:
For an acute angle, $\cos C>0$. Since side lengths are positive,
$$\begin{align*}c^2&=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C\\c^2&<a^2+b^2.\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $a^2+b^2$ is larger than $c^2$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: right

answer.worked:
For a right angle, $\cos90^\circ=0$.
$$\begin{align*}c^2&=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos90^\circ\\c^2&=a^2+b^2.\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $a^2+b^2$ equals $c^2$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: obtuse

answer.worked:
For an obtuse angle, $\cos C<0$, so $-2ab\cos C>0$.
$$\begin{align*}c^2&=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C\\c^2&>a^2+b^2.\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $a^2+b^2$ is smaller than $c^2$.

content.prompt: Suppose a set of points in the plane is such that the distance between any pair of these points is distinct. Prove that when each point is connected by a line segment to the point that is closest to it that no point is connected to more than five other points.

answer.short:
No point can be connected to six or more other points.

Two incident segments would form an angle at most $60^\circ$. The cosine rule makes the farther endpoint closer to the other endpoint than to the common point, contradicting the nearest-point connections.
answer.worked:
Suppose a point $A$ is connected to at least six other points. Two consecutive incident segments, $AB$ and $AC$, form an angle $\theta\leq60^\circ$, since the angles around $A$ sum to $360^\circ$.

Write $AB=b$ and $AC=c$, labelling the endpoints so that $b>c$; the distances are distinct. By the cosine rule,
$$\begin{align*}BC^2&=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos\theta\\BC^2&\leq b^2+c^2-2bc\cos60^\circ\\BC^2&\leq b^2+c^2-bc\\BC^2&\leq b^2+c(c-b)\\BC^2&<b^2.\end{align*}$$
Thus $BC<BA$, so $B$ cannot choose $A$ as its closest point. Also $AC<AB$, so $A$ cannot choose $B$ as its closest point. Therefore the segment $AB$ cannot be present, a contradiction. Hence every point is connected to at most five other points.

content.prompt: Suppose a convex quadrilateral has sides of length $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$, and diagonals of length $p$ and $q$.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Prove that the area of the quadrilateral is given by
$$A=\frac12pq\sin\theta,$$
where $\theta$ is the angle between the diagonals.

answer.short:
$A=\frac12pq\sin\theta$.

Split the quadrilateral along one diagonal and add the two triangle areas.
answer.worked:
Let the vertices in order be $V_1,V_2,V_3,V_4$, with successive sides $a,b,c,d$. Let the diagonals meet at $O$, where $V_2O=p_1$, $OV_4=p_2$, $V_1O=q_1$ and $OV_3=q_2$. Thus $p=p_1+p_2$ and $q=q_1+q_2$. Take $\theta=\angle V_1OV_2$; the supplementary angle has the same sine.

The triangles on opposite sides of diagonal $V_1V_3$ have heights $p_1\sin\theta$ and $p_2\sin\theta$.
$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac12qp_1\sin\theta+\frac12qp_2\sin\theta\\A&=\frac12q(p_1+p_2)\sin\theta\\A&=\frac12pq\sin\theta.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Prove that the area is also given by
$$A=\frac14\sqrt{4p^2q^2-(a^2+c^2-b^2-d^2)^2}.$$

answer.short:
$A=\frac14\sqrt{4p^2q^2-(a^2+c^2-b^2-d^2)^2}$.

Apply the cosine rule to the four triangles at the diagonal intersection, then use $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$.
answer.worked:
Use the notation from part (a). Adjacent angles at $O$ are supplementary, so $\cos(180^\circ-\theta)=-\cos\theta$. The cosine rule gives
$$\begin{align*}a^2&=p_1^2+q_1^2-2p_1q_1\cos\theta\\b^2&=p_1^2+q_2^2+2p_1q_2\cos\theta\\c^2&=p_2^2+q_2^2-2p_2q_2\cos\theta\\d^2&=p_2^2+q_1^2+2p_2q_1\cos\theta.\end{align*}$$
Subtracting and collecting terms,
$$\begin{align*}a^2+c^2-b^2-d^2&=-2(p_1q_1+p_1q_2+p_2q_1+p_2q_2)\cos\theta\\a^2+c^2-b^2-d^2&=-2(p_1+p_2)(q_1+q_2)\cos\theta\\a^2+c^2-b^2-d^2&=-2pq\cos\theta.\end{align*}$$
Using part (a),
$$\begin{align*}A^2&=\frac14p^2q^2\sin^2\theta\\A^2&=\frac14p^2q^2-\frac14p^2q^2\cos^2\theta\\A^2&=\frac14p^2q^2-\frac1{16}(a^2+c^2-b^2-d^2)^2\\A&=\frac14\sqrt{4p^2q^2-(a^2+c^2-b^2-d^2)^2}.\end{align*}$$
Take the positive square root because $A$ is an area.

children.label: c
children.prompt:
Prove that the area is also given by
$$A=\sqrt{\begin{aligned}&(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)\\&\quad-\frac14(ac+bd+pq)(ac+bd-pq)\end{aligned}},$$
where $s=\frac{a+b+c+d}{2}$ is the semi-perimeter.

answer.worked:
Write $\Delta=a^2+c^2-b^2-d^2$ and $T=ac+bd$. From part (b),
$$\begin{align*}A^2&=\frac14p^2q^2-\frac1{16}\Delta^2\\A^2&=\left(\frac14T^2-\frac1{16}\Delta^2\right)+\left(\frac14p^2q^2-\frac14T^2\right).\end{align*}$$
Factor the second bracket:
$$\begin{align*}\frac14p^2q^2-\frac14T^2&=-\frac14(T+pq)(T-pq)\\\frac14p^2q^2-\frac14T^2&=-\frac14(ac+bd+pq)(ac+bd-pq).\end{align*}$$
For the first bracket, let $K=\frac14T^2-\frac1{16}\Delta^2$.
$$\begin{align*}K&=\frac1{16}(2T-\Delta)(2T+\Delta)\\K&=\frac1{16}\big[(b+d)^2-(a-c)^2\big]\big[(a+c)^2-(b-d)^2\big]\\K&=\frac1{16}(b+d-a+c)(b+d+a-c)\\&\qquad\times(a+c-b+d)(a+c+b-d)\\K&=\frac1{16}\,[2(s-a)][2(s-c)][2(s-b)][2(s-d)]\\K&=(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d).\end{align*}$$
Substituting both results,
$$\begin{align*}A^2&=(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)\\&\qquad-\frac14(ac+bd+pq)(ac+bd-pq)\\A&=\sqrt{\begin{aligned}&(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)\\&\quad-\frac14(ac+bd+pq)(ac+bd-pq)\end{aligned}}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt:
Prove that if the quadrilateral is cyclic, then this simplifies to
$$A=\sqrt{(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)}.$$

answer.short:
$A=\sqrt{(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)}$.

Ptolemy’s theorem gives $pq=ac+bd$, so the correction term in part (c) is zero.
answer.worked:
For a cyclic quadrilateral, Ptolemy’s theorem gives $pq=ac+bd$. Hence $ac+bd-pq=0$. Substituting into part (c),
$$\begin{align*}A^2&=(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)-0\\A&=\sqrt{(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: Show that by setting $d=0$ the formula in part (c) reduces to Heron’s formula for the area of a triangle.

answer.short:
$A=\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$, where $s=\frac{a+b+c}{2}$.

When $d=0$, the quadrilateral becomes a triangle and $pq=ac$, so the correction term vanishes.
answer.worked:
Setting $d=0$ makes $V_4$ coincide with $V_1$. The remaining triangle has sides $a,b,c$, and the diagonals become $p=a$ and $q=c$. Thus
$$\begin{align*}\frac14(ac+bd+pq)(ac+bd-pq)&=\frac14(ac+ac)(ac-ac)\\\frac14(ac+bd+pq)(ac+bd-pq)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Also $s=\frac{a+b+c}{2}$ and $s-d=s$. Part (c) therefore becomes
$$\begin{align*}A^2&=s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)\\A&=\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)},\end{align*}$$
which is Heron’s formula.

children.prompt: Find the sector radius if the sector angle is $\frac{\pi}{6}$ and the area of the sector is $3\pi\text{ cm}^2$.

children.prompt: Find the perimeter of the sector whose area is $3\text{ cm}^2$ and whose arc length is $5\text{ cm}$.

answer.short:
$\frac{37}{5}\text{ cm}$

Use $A=\frac12rL$ to find the radius, then add the arc length and two radii.

Using $L=r\theta$ in the sector-area formula:
$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac12r^2\theta\\A&=\frac12rL\\3&=\frac12\times r\times5\\r&=\frac65\text{ cm}\\P&=L+2r\\P&=5+2\times\frac65\\P&=\frac{37}{5}\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Given that $OA=7$ and $AC=5$, determine the length of arc $AB$.

answer.worked:
Let $\theta=\angle AOC$, measured in radians. Since a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact,
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{5}{7}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)\\L&=7\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)\\L&\approx4.34.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Given that $OA=4$ and $BC=1$, determine the length of arc $AB$.

answer.worked:
Let $\theta=\angle AOC$, measured in radians. The tangent makes $\triangle OAC$ right-angled at $A$, and $OB=OA=4$.
$$\begin{align*}OC&=4+1=5\\\cos\theta&=\frac{4}{5}\\\theta&=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)\\L&=4\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)\\L&\approx2.57.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Given that $OA=2$ and the length of arc $AB$ is $1$, determine $OC$.

answer.worked:
Let $\theta=\angle AOC$, measured in radians. Use $L=r\theta$ and the right angle between the radius and tangent.
$$\begin{align*}1&=2\theta\\\theta&=\frac{1}{2}\\\cos\!\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)&=\frac{2}{OC}\\OC&=\frac{2}{\cos(1/2)}\\OC&\approx2.28.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Point $A$ is 1 kilometre from the edge of a circular lake of radius 1 kilometre. James runs a lap around the lake starting from point $A$, as indicated below. Find the length of his journey.

spec.description: External point A, two tangent journey segments and the major journey arc. Dashed centre line carries two consecutive labels 1; dashed radii meet the tangents at marked right angles. The source's decorative lake fill is omitted.
spec.mathematics: The lake radius is 1 km and the distance from its centre to A is 2 km. Tangency points are at central angles 30 and 150 degrees; the journey follows the remaining 240-degree arc.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied lengths and geometry are visible; no calculated lengths or angles are printed.

inlines.text: Add the two tangent lengths to the length of the major arc.

answer.worked:
Let $O$ be the lake's centre and $T,U$ the tangent contact points. A radius is perpendicular to a tangent at its point of contact, and the two tangents from $A$ have equal lengths.

$$\begin{align*}
AO&=1+1=2\\
AT&=\sqrt{2^2-1^2}\\
AT&=\sqrt{3}\\
\cos\angle TOA&=\frac{1}{2}\\
\angle TOA&=\frac{\pi}{3}\\
\angle TOU\text{ (minor)}&=2\times\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{2\pi}{3}\\
\theta\text{ (major)}&=2\pi-\frac{2\pi}{3}=\frac{4\pi}{3}\\
L&=r\theta=1\times\frac{4\pi}{3}=\frac{4\pi}{3}\\
\text{Journey length}&=2\sqrt{3}+\frac{4\pi}{3}\text{ km}
\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: **Distance to the horizon.** A lighthouse has a height of $d$ metres above sea level. The radius of the Earth is $r=6371$ kilometres. We are interested in measuring the length $l$ of the arc from the base of the lighthouse to a point on the horizon. In the formulas below, express $r$ and $d$ in the same units and measure $\theta$ in degrees.

spec.description: Earth cross-section with vertical lighthouse height segment, tangent to an upper-right horizon point, two radii, a derived right-angle marker and highlighted surface arc. The decorative lighthouse is replaced by its height segment.
spec.mathematics: The horizon radius is perpendicular to the sightline. The vertical centre-to-top distance is r+d; the central angle is theta and the intervening surface arc has length l. Diagram is schematic.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and geometric relationships are visible.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $\cos\theta=\dfrac{r}{r+d}$.

answer.worked:
The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the horizon, so the triangle is right-angled. With $r$ and $d$ expressed in the same units,
$$\begin{align*}\cos\theta&=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\\\cos\theta&=\frac{r}{r+d}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Explain why $l=\dfrac{\theta}{360}\times2\pi r$.

answer.short: The arc is $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of the circumference $2\pi r$, where $\theta$ is measured in degrees.
answer.worked:
An angle of $\theta$ degrees describes $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of a full revolution. The arc is the same fraction of the circumference:
$$l=\frac{\theta}{360}\times2\pi r.$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Given the lighthouse is $d=20$ metres tall, find the length $l$ of the arc to the nearest kilometre.

answer.short:
$16\text{ km}$.

Convert the height to kilometres, find $\theta$ using cosine, then calculate the arc length.
answer.worked:
Use $d=0.020\text{ km}$ and evaluate the inverse cosine in degrees. Keep the angle unrounded in the arc calculation.
$$\begin{align*}\cos\theta&=\frac{6371}{6371+0.020}\\\theta&=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{6371}{6371.020}\right)\\l&=\frac{\cos^{-1}(6371/6371.020)}{360}\times2\pi\times6371\\l&\approx15.96368796\text{ km}\\l&\approx16\text{ km}\quad\text{(nearest kilometre).}\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Given the arc length to the horizon is $l=20\text{ km}$, find the height $d$ of the lighthouse to the nearest metre.

answer.short:
$31\text{ m}$.

Find the central angle from the arc length, then rearrange the cosine relation.
answer.worked:
Use kilometres throughout the calculation and evaluate cosine in degrees.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=\frac{20\times360}{2\pi\times6371}\\6371+d&=\frac{6371}{\cos\theta}\\d&=\frac{6371}{\cos\theta}-6371\\d&\approx0.03139237502\text{ km}\\d&\approx31.39237502\text{ m}\\d&\approx31\text{ m}\quad\text{(nearest metre).}\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$48-8\pi-20\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac43\right)$ square units, with the inverse tangent evaluated in radians.

Subtract the three sectors from the triangle formed by the circle centres.
answer.worked:
Join the three centres. Their triangle has side lengths $10$, $10$ and $12$. Let its height be $h$ and each base angle be $\alpha$, measured in radians.

$$\begin{align*}h&=\sqrt{10^2-6^2}\\h&=8\\\alpha&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac86\right)\\\alpha&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac43\right).\end{align*}$$

The angle at the upper centre is $\pi-2\alpha$. The required gap is the triangle minus the three sectors.

$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac12(12)(8)-2\left(\frac12\cdot6^2\alpha\right)-\frac12\cdot4^2(\pi-2\alpha)\\A&=48-36\alpha-8\pi+16\alpha\\A&=48-8\pi-20\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac43\right)\text{ square units}.\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Find the percentage of the silo that he can see, correct to the nearest whole percentage.

answer.short:
$25\%$.

The tangent sightlines bound the visible arc.
answer.worked:
Let $O$ be the centre and $A$ a point where a sightline from $T$ touches the silo. Since a tangent is perpendicular to the radius, $\triangle OAT$ is right-angled at $A$. Let $\theta=\angle AOT$, measured in radians.

The two tangent sightlines bound a visible arc with central angle $2\theta$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Visible percentage}&=\frac{2\theta}{2\pi}\times100\%\\\text{Visible percentage}&=\frac{100}{\pi}\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)\%\\\text{Visible percentage}&\approx24.68\%\\\text{Visible percentage}&\approx25\%\quad\text{(nearest whole percentage).}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the distance from the silo (to the nearest metre) that Tom should stand so that he can see $40\%$ of the silo.

answer.short:
$11\text{ m}$ from the silo.

Use half the visible central angle in the right triangle formed by a radius and a tangent sightline.
answer.worked:

$$\begin{align*}\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}\right)&=\frac{5}{5+d}\\5+d&=\frac{5}{\cos(2\pi/5)}\\d&=\frac{5}{\cos(2\pi/5)}-5\\d&\approx11.18\text{ m}\\d&\approx11\text{ m}\quad\text{(nearest metre).}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
A chord splits a circle into two regions of area $a$ and $b$. The segment associated with the central angle $\theta$ has area $a$, where $\theta$ is measured in radians. Show that
$$\theta=\sin\theta+\frac{2a\pi}{a+b}.$$

answer.worked:
Let the circle have radius $r$. The segment area is the sector area minus the triangle area:
$$\begin{align*}a&=\frac12r^2\theta-\frac12r^2\sin\theta\\a&=\frac12r^2(\theta-\sin\theta).\end{align*}$$
The two regions together form the whole circle:
$$\begin{align*}a+b&=\pi r^2\\r^2&=\frac{a+b}{\pi}.\end{align*}$$
Substituting into the segment-area formula gives
$$\begin{align*}a&=\frac{a+b}{2\pi}(\theta-\sin\theta)\\\frac{2a\pi}{a+b}&=\theta-\sin\theta\\\theta&=\sin\theta+\frac{2a\pi}{a+b}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the length of the shortest string that can be wrapped around the circles.

inlines.text: Add the two tangent lengths and the exterior arcs; the inverse cosine is in radians.

answer.worked:
Let $\theta$ be the angle between the centre line and the larger radius to an upper tangent point, measured in radians. The radii are perpendicular to the tangent. If each straight string segment has length $d$, then
$$\begin{align*}d^2&=(a+b)^2-(a-b)^2\\d^2&=4ab\\d&=2\sqrt{ab}.\end{align*}$$
The corresponding right triangle gives
$$\begin{align*}\cos\theta&=\frac{a-b}{a+b}\\\theta&=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{a-b}{a+b}\right).\end{align*}$$
The exterior arcs have angles $2\pi-2\theta$ and $2\theta$. Using $L=r\theta$, the total length is
$$\begin{align*}L&=a(2\pi-2\theta)+2b\theta+2d\\L&=2\pi a-2(a-b)\theta+4\sqrt{ab}\\L&=2\pi a+4\sqrt{ab}-2(a-b)\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{a-b}{a+b}\right).\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Suppose $a=b$. What does your expression in (a) simplify to?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}L&=2\pi a+4\sqrt{a^2}-2(a-a)\cos^{-1}(0)\\L&=(2\pi+4)a.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c

answer.worked:
As $b\to0$, $\sqrt{ab}\to0$ and $\cos^{-1}((a-b)/(a+b))\to\cos^{-1}(1)=0$. Hence
$$\begin{align*}L&\to2\pi a+0-2a\times0\\L&\to2\pi a.\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the radius of the sector of perimeter 4 that has maximal area. (Assume the sector does not comprise the entire circle.)

answer.short:
$r=1$.

Express the area as a quadratic in $r$; its maximum occurs midway between its zeros.
answer.worked:
Let $\theta$ be the central angle in radians.
$$\begin{align*}2r+r\theta&=4\\r\theta&=4-2r\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac12r^2\theta\\A&=\frac12r(4-2r)\\A&=-r(r-2)\end{align*}$$
This quadratic opens downwards and has zeros at $r=0$ and $r=2$. Its maximum occurs halfway between them, at $r=1$. Here $\theta=2<2\pi$, so the sector is not the entire circle.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the radius of the sector of area 16 that has minimal perimeter. (Assume the sector does not comprise the entire circle.)

answer.short:
$r=4$.

Use AM–GM on $P=2r+32/r$; equality occurs when $2r=32/r$.
answer.worked:
Let $\theta$ be the central angle in radians.
$$\begin{align*}\frac12r^2\theta&=16\\\theta&=\frac{32}{r^2}\end{align*}$$
By the AM–GM inequality,
$$\begin{align*}P&=2r+r\theta\\P&=2r+\frac{32}{r}\\P&\ge 2\sqrt{(2r)\left(\frac{32}{r}\right)}\\P&\ge16.\end{align*}$$
Equality occurs when the two positive terms are equal:
$$\begin{align*}2r&=\frac{32}{r}\\r^2&=16\\r&=4.\end{align*}$$
Thus the minimum perimeter occurs at $r=4$. Here $\theta=2<2\pi$, so the sector is not the entire circle.

children.prompt: Using this fact, prove that $$\cos\theta\leq\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}\leq\frac{1}{\cos\theta}.$$

answer.short:
$\cos\theta\leq\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\theta}\leq\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$.

Compare the triangle and sector areas, then divide by positive quantities.
answer.worked:
Since $OA=OD=1$, $OB=\cos\theta$, $AB=\sin\theta$ and $DC=\tan\theta$.

$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{area}(\triangle AOB)&=\frac12\sin\theta\cos\theta\\\operatorname{area}(\operatorname{sector}(AOD))&=\frac12\theta\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle COD)&=\frac12\tan\theta.\end{align*}$$

The given area comparison gives
$$\frac12\sin\theta\cos\theta\leq\frac12\theta\leq\frac12\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}.$$
Dividing by $\frac12\sin\theta>0$ gives
$$\cos\theta\leq\frac{\theta}{\sin\theta}\leq\frac1{\cos\theta}.$$
Taking reciprocals reverses the inequalities, so
$$\cos\theta\leq\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}\leq\frac1{\cos\theta}.$$

answer.short:
$\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\theta}\to1$.

It is squeezed between $\cos\theta$ and $1/\cos\theta$, which both approach $1$.
answer.worked: As $\theta$ approaches $0$, both $\cos\theta$ and $\dfrac1{\cos\theta}$ approach $1$. By part (a), $\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\theta}$ lies between these quantities, so it also approaches $1$.

content.prompt: A regular $n$-sided polygon is inscribed in a circle of radius $r$. The side length of the polygon is denoted by $s$, and the distance from the centre of the circle to any side of the polygon is denoted by $a$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find an expression for $r$ in terms of $s$.

answer.worked:
Join the centre to the endpoints of one side and bisect the resulting isosceles triangle. The right triangle has angle $\pi/n$, opposite side $s/2$ and hypotenuse $r$.
$$\begin{align*}\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right)&=\frac{s}{2r}\\r&=\frac{s}{2\sin(\pi/n)}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find an expression for $r$ in terms of $a$.

answer.worked:
In the same right triangle, the adjacent side is $a$ and the hypotenuse is $r$.
$$\begin{align*}\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right)&=\frac{a}{r}\\r&=\frac{a}{\cos(\pi/n)}.\end{align*}$$

children.prompt:

answer.short:
$A_n=\dfrac12nr^2\sin(2\pi/n)$.

Divide the polygon into $n$ congruent triangles with two sides $r$ and included angle $2\pi/n$.
answer.worked:
Joining the centre to every vertex divides the polygon into $n$ congruent triangles. Each has two sides of length $r$ and included angle $2\pi/n$.
$$\begin{align*}A_n&=n\left(\frac12r\cdot r\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{n}\right)\right)\\A_n&=\frac12nr^2\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{n}\right).\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Prove that $A_n$ approaches $\pi r^2$ as $n$ approaches $\infty$. Hint: Use your answer to the previous exercise.

answer.short:
$A_n\to\pi r^2$.

Write $A_n=\pi r^2(\sin u/u)$, where $u=2\pi/n$, and use $\sin u/u\to1$ as $u\to0$.
answer.worked:
Let $u=2\pi/n$.
$$\begin{align*}A_n&=\frac12nr^2\sin u\\A_n&=\pi r^2\frac{\sin u}{u}.\end{align*}$$
As $n\to\infty$, $u\to0$. The previous exercise gives $\sin u/u\to1$, so
$$A_n\to\pi r^2.$$
Thus the polygon's area approaches the circle's area.

content.prompt: A point is randomly chosen inside of a unit square (uniformly). Find the probability that the point is less than 1 unit away from all four vertices of the square.

inlines.text: Find the area common to the four unit-radius quarter circles; the unit square has area 1.

answer.worked:
The required region is the intersection of four quarter circles of radius 1, centred at the square's vertices. Since the square has area 1, its area equals the required probability.

Take the square's vertices as $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(1,1)$ and $(0,1)$. The four boundary junctions are $(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2})$, $(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\tfrac12)$, $(\tfrac12,1-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2})$ and $(1-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\tfrac12)$. Joining them forms a square with both diagonals of length $\sqrt3-1$. Each of the four remaining circular segments subtends $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$ at its centre.

$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{inner square}}&=\frac12(\sqrt3-1)^2\\A_{\text{inner square}}&=2-\sqrt3\\A_{\text{segment}}&=\frac12\left(\frac{\pi}{6}-\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\\A_{\text{segment}}&=\frac{\pi}{12}-\frac14\\P&=(2-\sqrt3)+4\left(\frac{\pi}{12}-\frac14\right)\\P&=1+\frac{\pi}{3}-\sqrt3\end{align*}$$

entries.description: In this chapter we are concerned with right-angled triangles. A second angle in such a triangle is often denoted by the Greek letter theta, denoted by the symbol θ. This can indicate both the name and the measure of the angle. The hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle always refers to the side that is opposite the right angle. The other two sides are named according to their positions relative to angle θ. The opposite side is opposite angle θ, while the adjacent side is next to angle θ.

entries.description: Roughly speaking, two triangles with the same angles will also have the same shape. By this, we mean that the two triangles will be similar. In particular, the ratios of their corresponding sides are equal. We prove this below in the special case that our two triangles are right-angled.

entries.description:
Theorem 1 (The trigonometric ratios)
If two right-angled triangles have equal angles, then the ratios of their corresponding sides are equal.

entries.description: Take two copies of the first triangle and two copies of the second, and arrange these into the rectangle shown below. The area below the diagonal is the same as the area above the diagonal. Therefore, we can eliminate one copy of each triangle from above and below the diagonal, and the area that remains above the diagonal will equal the area that remains below the diagonal. Therefore, \(aO=oA\). It follows that \(\frac{o}{a}=\frac{O}{A}\).

entries.description:
We now know that for any right-angled triangle with given angle θ, the ratios O/H and A/H and O/A are fixed. These fixed ratios are given the following names.
\(\sin\theta=\frac{O}{H}\) The sine of θ equals opposite over hypotenuse.
\(\cos\theta=\frac{A}{H}\) The cosine of θ equals adjacent over hypotenuse.
\(\tan\theta=\frac{O}{A}\) The tangent of θ equals opposite over adjacent.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone definitions; reference evidence only.

entries.description:
We first use the Pythagorean Theorem to establish the length of the side opposite to θ. Let us denote this side length by x. We have
\(x^2+2^2=3^2\)
\(x^2+4=9\)
\(x^2=5\)
\(x=\sqrt{5}\).
Therefore,
\(\sin\theta=\frac{O}{H}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\), \(\cos\theta=\frac{A}{H}=\frac{2}{3}\), \(\tan\theta=\frac{O}{A}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\).

entries.description: A flagpole is stabilised by two cables affixed to the top of the pole. The first of these makes a 40° degree angle to the ground and is 5.5 metres long. The second makes an angle of 50° to the ground. How long is the second cable?

entries.description:
Let y be the height of the flagpole and let x be the length of the second cable.
Using the sine ratio for both triangles, we find that
sin 40° = y/5.5; sin 50° = y/x.
y = 5.5 sin 40° (1); y = x sin 50° (2).
Equating (1) and (2) gives
x sin 50° = 5.5 sin 40°
x = (5.5 sin 40°)/(sin 50°)
≈ 4.62.
The second cable is approximately 4.62 metres long.

entries.description:
The two unknowns d and h must be solved using simultaneous equations. From △ACD we see that
\[\tan\alpha=\frac{h}{d+210}\]
\[h=(d+210)\tan\alpha\qquad(1)\]
From △BCD we see that
\[\tan\beta=\frac{h}{d}\]
\[h=d\tan\beta\qquad(2)\]
Equating (1) and (2) gives
\[\begin{aligned}d\tan\beta&=(d+210)\tan\alpha\\d\tan\beta&=d\tan\alpha+210\tan\alpha\\d\tan\beta-d\tan\alpha&=210\tan\alpha\\d(\tan\beta-\tan\alpha)&=210\tan\alpha\\d&=\frac{210\tan\alpha}{\tan\beta-\tan\alpha}.\end{aligned}\]
Therefore,
\[\begin{aligned}h&=d\tan\beta\\&=\frac{210\tan\alpha\tan\beta}{\tan\beta-\tan\alpha}\\&=\frac{210\tan28^\circ\tan42^\circ}{\tan42^\circ-\tan28^\circ}\\&\approx273\text{ m}.\end{aligned}\]

entries.description:
Case 1. Suppose C is acute. Draw an altitude BD of length h. The altitude must lie within the triangle. Applying the Pythagorean Theorem to both triangles BCD and ABD gives
h² = a² − y² and h² = c² − (b − y)².
We equate these to give a² − y² = c² − (b − y)². Therefore,
c² = a² + (b − y)² − y²
= a² + b² − 2by + y² − y²
= a² + b² − 2by
= a² + b² − 2ab cos C.

entries.description:
Case 2. Now suppose C is obtuse. The altitude BD lies outside △ABC. Applying the Pythagorean Theorem to both triangles BCD and ABD gives
h² = a² − y² and h² = c² − (b + y)².
As before, we equate these to give a² − y² = c² − (b + y)². Therefore,
c² = a² + (b + y)² − y²
= a² + b² + 2by + y² − y²
= a² + b² + 2by
= a² + b² + 2ab cos(180° − C).

entries.description:
A sector is a region within a circle enclosed by two radii and an arc. To find the area of a sector we multiply the fraction of a revolution described by the sector by the area of the entire circle. When working in degrees we obtain:
 L = θ/360° × (πr²) = πθr²/360°.
When working in radians we obtain:
 L = θ/(2π) × (πr²) = ½θr².
